q: Name the pinned ganglion.
options: Celiac ganglion
Superior cervical ganglion
Inferior mesenteric ganglion
Superior mesenteric ganglion

fig.alt: A drawing of the brainstem and spinal cord from the front, with the segments labeled from the pons down to S5 and a column of ganglia beside the cord on each side. Solid lines leave the cord only between T1 and L2. Some run to the chain of ganglia beside the cord, and some run past it as the greater and lesser splanchnic nerves to three round ganglia in front of the spine: the celiac, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric ganglia. Dashed lines run from the ganglia to a column of organs on the right, from the eye, tear gland and saliva glands at the top through the heart, airways, stomach, liver, pancreas, adrenal gland and intestines to the bladder and genitals at the bottom. A patch of skin on the left is supplied from the chain.

q: Name the pinned connecting branch between the spinal nerve and the chain ganglion.
options: Gray ramus communicans
White ramus communicans
Splanchnic nerve
Ventral ramus of the spinal nerve

fig.alt: Three panels, each pairing a small schematic with a three-dimensional drawing of a spinal cord cross section, its spinal nerve and the neighboring sympathetic chain ganglion. In the top panel a red fiber leaves the lateral horn, enters the chain through the white ramus communicans and synapses in the ganglion at the same level. In the middle panel the fiber climbs the chain to synapse in a higher ganglion, and postganglionic fibers return to spinal nerves through gray rami communicantes. In the bottom panel the fiber passes through the chain without synapsing and runs in a splanchnic nerve to a prevertebral ganglion, where it synapses.

q: Name the pinned branches.
options: White rami communicantes
Dorsal roots
Gray rami communicantes
Postganglionic fibers

fig.alt: Three panels, each pairing a small schematic with a three-dimensional drawing of a spinal cord cross section, its spinal nerve and the neighboring sympathetic chain ganglion. In the top panel a red fiber leaves the lateral horn, enters the chain through the white ramus communicans and synapses in the ganglion at the same level. In the middle panel the fiber climbs the chain to synapse in a higher ganglion, and postganglionic fibers return to spinal nerves through gray rami communicantes. In the bottom panel the fiber passes through the chain without synapsing and runs in a splanchnic nerve to a prevertebral ganglion, where it synapses.

q: Name the pinned ganglion, where fibers of cranial nerve III synapse.
options: Otic ganglion
Superior cervical ganglion
Pterygopalatine ganglion
Ciliary ganglion

fig.alt: The same brainstem, spinal cord and organ column as the sympathetic map, now showing parasympathetic fibers in blue. From four shaded brainstem nuclei, fibers run out in cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X. Nerves III, VII and IX end in small circled ganglia near the eye, the tear and nasal glands and the saliva glands. Nerve X sweeps down to the heart, airways, stomach, liver, pancreas and intestines. From the lowest sacral segments, a second group of blue fibers runs to the colon, rectum, bladder and genitals. The red sympathetic chain is drawn faintly beside the cord for comparison.

q: Where are the cell bodies of sympathetic preganglionic neurons?
options: In the brainstem and in sacral segments S2–S4
In the lateral horn of the spinal cord, segments T1–L2
In the chain ganglia beside the vertebral column
In the ventral horn at every spinal segment

q: Which cranial nerves carry parasympathetic preganglionic fibers?
options: III, VII, IX and X
V, VII, IX and X
III, IV, VI, VII and X
I, II, VIII and X

q: Put the steps in order to trace a sympathetic signal from the spinal cord to a sweat gland in the skin of your forearm.
options: A preganglionic neuron fires in the lateral horn of an upper thoracic segment
Its axon leaves in the ventral root and enters the spinal nerve
The axon passes through a white ramus communicans into the sympathetic chain
It synapses on a postganglionic neuron in a chain ganglion
The postganglionic axon returns to a spinal nerve through a gray ramus communicans
The postganglionic axon reaches the sweat gland in the forearm skin

q: Put the steps in order to trace the sympathetic pathway through the adrenal medulla.
options: A preganglionic neuron fires in the lateral horn of a thoracic segment
Its axon passes through a white ramus and through the chain without synapsing
The axon runs in a splanchnic nerve and passes through the celiac ganglion without synapsing
The axon synapses on chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla
Chromaffin cells release epinephrine and some norepinephrine into the blood
The blood carries epinephrine to cells throughout the body

q: Select every feature of the parasympathetic division.
options: Preganglionic fibers leave in cranial nerves and from S2–S4
Ganglia sit near or inside the target organ
Postganglionic fibers reach the skin through gray rami communicantes
Preganglionic fibers are long and postganglionic fibers are short
A preganglionic neuron branches to many chain ganglia
The vagus nerve carries most of its preganglionic fibers

q: A fiber is traced in the gray ramus that joins spinal nerve C6. What kind of fiber is it most likely to be?
options: A sympathetic preganglionic fiber entering the chain
A parasympathetic postganglionic fiber heading to the arm
A somatic motor fiber heading to an arm muscle
An unmyelinated sympathetic postganglionic fiber returning from the chain

q: Mr. Okafor, 61, has a tumor at the very top of his right lung, beside the upper thoracic vertebrae. His right pupil is smaller than his left, his right upper eyelid droops slightly, and the right side of his face does not sweat. Which structure has the tumor most likely damaged?
options: The right oculomotor nerve
The right sympathetic chain
The right vagus nerve
The right facial nerve

q: A student traced a sympathetic signal to the stomach. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: A preganglionic neuron fires in the lateral horn at T7
Its axon enters the chain through a white ramus communicans
It synapses in the chain ganglion at T7
It runs in the greater splanchnic nerve to the celiac ganglion
A postganglionic fiber from the celiac ganglion reaches the stomach

q: Complete the pathway: lateral horn → white ramus → through the chain → splanchnic nerve → ____ → epinephrine released into the blood.
options: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla
Postganglionic neurons in the celiac ganglion
A gray ramus communicans
Cells of the outer layer of the adrenal gland

q: Why does a burst of sympathetic activity reach many organs at once, while parasympathetic activity can affect one organ at a time?
options: Sympathetic fibers are myelinated all the way to the target, so their signal spreads farther
The sympathetic division has more preganglionic neurons than there are organs to supply
Sympathetic preganglionic neurons branch widely through the chain
Parasympathetic postganglionic fibers are too long to reach more than one organ

q: After a transplant, a heart has no nerve connections at all. Unlike a skeletal muscle that loses its nerve, it keeps contracting. Which feature of autonomic motor pathways does this illustrate?
options: Autonomic effectors have their own activity, which the nerves speed up or slow down
Autonomic signals travel through two neurons, so one cut neuron is replaced by the other
Autonomic nerves regrow within hours after being cut
Heart muscle is controlled by somatic motor neurons that are not cut in surgery
misconception: autonomic effectors stop working without their nerves

q: A diver breaks his neck and completely cuts his spinal cord at C6. Which autonomic pathway from his brain to his heart is still intact?
options: Sympathetic fibers leaving the cord at T1–T4
Sympathetic fibers that pass through the superior cervical ganglion
Parasympathetic fibers in the vagus nerve
Parasympathetic fibers leaving the cord at S2–S4

q: Where are the parasympathetic ganglia that supply the wall of the stomach?
options: In the celiac ganglion in front of the vertebral column
In the sympathetic chain beside the vertebrae
In the dorsal root ganglia
In the stomach wall itself

q: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla are best compared with which cells?
options: Preganglionic neurons in the lateral horn
Sympathetic postganglionic neurons without axons
Parasympathetic terminal ganglion cells
Somatic motor neurons

q: A frightening near-miss in traffic triggers a sympathetic burst. Your heart is still pounding minutes after the nerve activity has died down. Which feature of the sympathetic division best explains this?
options: Postganglionic fibers are unmyelinated and conduct slowly
Gray rami carry signals only to the skin
Epinephrine released into the blood keeps acting after the nerve signal stops
Preganglionic fibers are short

q: During pelvic surgery, the pelvic splanchnic nerves on both sides are injured. Which organ loses parasympathetic supply?
options: The stomach
The heart
The saliva gland in front of the ear
The urinary bladder

q: Select every target that receives sympathetic fibers but no parasympathetic fibers.
options: Sweat glands in the skin
Arrector pili muscles
The adrenal medulla
The heart
Smooth muscle in most blood vessel walls
The iris

q: Which autonomic neurons release acetylcholine?
options: Only parasympathetic neurons, both preganglionic and postganglionic
All preganglionic neurons, all parasympathetic postganglionic neurons, and sympathetic postganglionic neurons to sweat glands
All postganglionic neurons of both the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions
Only the preganglionic neurons that end on the adrenal medulla

q: On a hot day, sympathetic activity makes you sweat. Which transmitter and receptor protein act on the eccrine sweat glands?
options: Norepinephrine on alpha-1 adrenergic receptor proteins
Epinephrine on beta-2 receptor proteins
Acetylcholine on muscarinic receptor proteins
Acetylcholine on nicotinic receptor proteins

q: A patient starts taking metoprolol, a beta blocker that acts mainly on beta-1 receptor proteins. Predict the change in each variable at rest, compared with before the drug.
A patient is given atropine, a muscarinic antagonist. Predict the change in each variable, compared with before the drug.

variables.name: Movement of the stomach and intestine wall

q: A student with narrowed airways inhales albuterol, a beta-2 agonist. Predict the change in each variable over the next 15 minutes.

variables.name: Tension in the smooth muscle of the small airway walls

q: A farmworker is poisoned by an organophosphate insecticide, which blocks acetylcholinesterase. He is drooling and sweating, his pupils are pinpoint, his heart rate is slow, his airways are filling with secretions, and his muscles twitch and grow weak. He is given atropine. Which problem will atropine not fix?
options: The heart rate of 42 beats per minute
The drooling
The airway secretions
The muscle twitching and weakness

q: A child eats berries of deadly nightshade, which contain a muscarinic antagonist. Select every sign you would expect.
options: Hot, dry skin
Widened pupils
A fast heart rate
Heavy drooling
Dry mouth
Pinpoint pupils

q: Ms. Reyes has a lung condition in which her small airways narrow easily. Days after starting propranolol for her blood pressure, she becomes short of breath and wheezy. What is the most likely cause?
options: Propranolol activated her alpha-1 receptor proteins
Propranolol blocked the beta-2 receptor proteins on her airway smooth muscle
Propranolol blocked muscarinic receptor proteins in her airways
Propranolol slowed her heart so much that fluid backed up into her lungs

q: During a sprint, why do the small airways widen more once the adrenal medulla is releasing its hormone than with sympathetic nerve activity alone?
options: Epinephrine binds beta-2 receptor proteins far better than norepinephrine
Epinephrine blocks muscarinic receptor proteins in the airways
The adrenal medulla releases acetylcholine onto the airways
Norepinephrine from nerves activates alpha-1 receptor proteins, which widen the airways

q: Clonidine activates alpha-2 receptor proteins, including those on adrenergic varicosities. What happens to norepinephrine release from those varicosities?
options: It rises, because alpha-2 receptor proteins open calcium channels in the varicosity membrane
It is unchanged, because alpha-2 receptor proteins sit only on smooth muscle
It falls, because alpha-2 receptor proteins on the varicosity inhibit further release
It rises briefly and then stops for good

q: Nicotine activates nicotinic receptor proteins in every autonomic ganglion, so it stimulates both divisions. Yet in a smoker, the small arteries of the skin clearly constrict. Why does the sympathetic effect win in these vessels?
options: Nicotine blocks the parasympathetic ganglia at the same time as it stimulates the sympathetic ganglia
Skin vessels receive only sympathetic fibers, so there is no parasympathetic effect to oppose it
Parasympathetic fibers release norepinephrine onto skin vessels
Nicotine binds alpha-1 receptor proteins directly

q: Put the steps in order to show how a sympathetic signal constricts a small artery in the skin.
options: A preganglionic neuron releases acetylcholine in a chain ganglion
Acetylcholine binds nicotinic receptor proteins and depolarizes the postganglionic neuron
Action potentials reach the varicosities and calcium enters
Norepinephrine is released and binds alpha-1 receptor proteins on the smooth muscle
Calcium rises inside the smooth muscle cells and they contract
The vessel narrows

q: A student described how the vagus nerve slows the heart. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: A vagal preganglionic neuron releases acetylcholine in a terminal ganglion in the heart wall
Acetylcholine binds nicotinic receptor proteins on the postganglionic neuron
The postganglionic neuron releases norepinephrine onto the heart's pacemaker tissue
The transmitter binds muscarinic receptor proteins, and potassium channels open
The cells hyperpolarize and take longer to reach threshold

q: Complete the sequence: epinephrine binds beta-1 receptor proteins on heart muscle → a G protein is activated → ____ → more calcium enters the cell → each contraction is stronger.
options: Cyclic AMP rises inside the cell
Potassium channels open
Acetylcholine is released
The cell hyperpolarizes

q: An eye doctor puts phenylephrine drops, an alpha-1 agonist, into your eyes before an exam. What happens to your pupils, and why?
options: They narrow, because the circular iris muscle contracts
They do not change, because the iris has no adrenergic receptor proteins
They narrow, because the dilator muscle relaxes
They widen, because the radial dilator muscle contracts

q: What kind of receptor protein is the nicotinic receptor protein on a postganglionic neuron?
options: A G protein–coupled receptor
A ligand-gated channel that lets sodium in
A voltage-gated calcium channel
An enzyme that splits acetylcholine

q: In an old treatment for dangerously raised blood pressure, a drug blocked nicotinic receptor proteins in every autonomic ganglion. Why did blood pressure fall so sharply?
options: The drug blocked the heart's muscarinic receptor proteins
The drug paralyzed skeletal muscle, which stopped pumping blood through the veins
The drug made the adrenal medulla release more epinephrine
Vessels lost their ongoing sympathetic constriction

q: Two patients need a beta blocker. One has a lung condition in which the small airways narrow easily. Which choice fits that patient better, and why?
options: Metoprolol, because it acts mainly on beta-1 receptor proteins
Propranolol, because blocking beta-2 relaxes airway smooth muscle
Propranolol, because it acts only on the heart
Metoprolol, because it activates beta-2 receptor proteins

q: Select every location of nicotinic receptor proteins.
options: Cell bodies of sympathetic postganglionic neurons
Cell bodies of parasympathetic postganglionic neurons
Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla
Smooth muscle of the stomach wall
The motor end plate of skeletal muscle
Cells of the heart's pacemaker tissue

q: Mr. Adeyemi has a severe allergic reaction: his blood pressure is falling and his airways are closing. The paramedic injects epinephrine. Which receptor protein is responsible for reopening his airways?
options: Alpha-1
Beta-2
Beta-1
Muscarinic

q: A patient with glaucoma is prescribed pilocarpine eye drops, a muscarinic agonist. What will the drops do to her pupil?
options: Widen it, by relaxing the dilator muscle
Widen it, by relaxing the circular muscle
Narrow it, by contracting the circular muscle
Leave it unchanged, because pilocarpine acts only on the lens

q: Mr. Chen takes his first dose of prazosin, an alpha-1 antagonist, and feels faint when he stands up quickly. What best explains this?
options: His heart cannot speed up, because beta-1 receptor proteins are blocked
Alpha-1 blockade stops his vessels from constricting when he stands
His vagus nerve is overactive, because muscarinic receptor proteins are stimulated
His airways narrow, lowering the oxygen reaching his brain

q: Norepinephrine makes the smooth muscle of skin vessels contract, but epinephrine makes the smooth muscle of skeletal muscle vessels relax. What is the best explanation?
options: Epinephrine and norepinephrine carry opposite instructions
Skeletal muscle vessels receive parasympathetic fibers that override the signal
The vessels carry different receptor proteins: alpha-1 or beta-2
Skin vessels lack receptor proteins altogether

q: Which of these effectors does not have dual innervation?
options: The heart
The iris
The smooth muscle of skin blood vessels
The muscle in the wall of the stomach

q: In a resting adult, atropine raises the heart rate by about 30 beats a minute, but a beta blocker lowers it by only a few beats. What does this show?
options: At rest, vagal tone on the heart is much stronger than its sympathetic tone
The heart carries no beta-1 receptor proteins while the body is at rest
Atropine directly stimulates beta-1 receptor proteins
The sympathetic division is silent at rest

q: A patient is given an injection of phenylephrine, an alpha-1 agonist, into a vein. Predict each variable, first as the direct effect of the drug, before any reflex acts, and then about a minute later, once autonomic reflexes have acted. Compare each with the value before the injection.

variables.name: Diameter of skin blood vessels, direct drug effect
Vagal output to the heart, a minute later

q: A dog suddenly lunges at a jogger from behind a fence. Predict the change in each variable across her body over the next minute.

variables.name: Glucose released into the blood by the liver
Movement of the stomach and intestine wall

q: The small vessels in the skin of your fingers have no parasympathetic supply. How does your nervous system widen them when you warm up?
options: It sends acetylcholine to them through the vagus nerve
It lowers sympathetic tone, so the vessels constrict less
It raises sympathetic tone, which widens them through alpha-1 receptor proteins
It cannot widen them; only local heat can
misconception: an organ needs two opposing nerves to be turned both up and down

q: Six months after a heart transplant, Mr. Novak's resting heart rate is 100 beats a minute, though he is calm and well. Before surgery, his resting rate was 68. What best explains the change?
options: His new heart has an unusually high number of beta-1 receptor proteins
Cutting the nerves raised his sympathetic tone
His new heart receives no vagal tone, so it beats at its own rate
His adrenal medulla now releases epinephrine continuously

q: Put the steps of the pupillary light reflex in order, starting with light shone into one eye.
options: Light strikes the retina and retinal ganglion cells fire
Signals travel along the optic nerve to the pretectal nuclei in the midbrain
The pretectal nuclei stimulate the Edinger–Westphal nuclei on both sides
Preganglionic fibers travel in both oculomotor nerves to the ciliary ganglia
Postganglionic fibers release acetylcholine onto the circular iris muscle
Both pupils narrow

q: Ms. Tran's right oculomotor nerve is compressed after a head injury. A penlight is shone into her right eye. What happens to her pupils?
options: Both pupils narrow normally
Neither pupil narrows
The right pupil narrows, but the left pupil stays wide
The left pupil narrows but the right does not

q: A student described the reflex that follows standing up quickly. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: Blood pools in the legs and pressure in the large arteries dips
Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the artery walls fire less
Fewer signals reach the medulla oblongata through nerves IX and X
The medulla oblongata increases vagal output and decreases sympathetic output
Heart rate rises and the vessels in the skin and gut constrict

q: Complete the visceral reflex arc: sensory receptor → visceral sensory neuron → integration center in the CNS → preganglionic neuron → ____ → postganglionic neuron → effector.
options: Autonomic ganglion
Dorsal root ganglion
Neuromuscular junction
Ventral horn

q: Select every effect of strong sympathetic activation.
options: Blood vessels in the skin narrow
The liver releases glucose into the blood
The pupils narrow
Sweating increases
Gut movement speeds up
The small airways widen

q: An hour after a large meal, parasympathetic activity dominates. Select every effect you would expect.
options: Slower heart rate
More movement and secretion in the stomach and intestines
Widened pupils
Relaxed sphincters along the gut
Glucose released from liver glycogen
Increased sweating

q: Before giving a speech, a student's mouth feels dry and sticky. Which statement explains this?
options: Sympathetic activity stops all saliva secretion
Parasympathetic activity is increased by feeling nervous before speaking
Sympathetic activity adds thick saliva as watery secretion falls
The glands that make saliva have no autonomic supply

q: Which brain region is the main integrator of autonomic function, linking emotions, body temperature and water balance to autonomic output?
options: Cerebellum
Hypothalamus
Primary motor cortex
Thalamus

q: A healthy medical student faints the first time she watches blood being drawn. Just before she faints, her heart rate falls and her face turns pale. Which pathway best explains this?
options: The limbic system triggers a vagal burst and a fall in sympathetic tone
A spinal visceral reflex is triggered by stretch in the arm used for the blood draw
Her adrenal medulla releases a surge of epinephrine
Her cerebellum loses control of posture

q: An emergency physician checks a patient's pupillary light reflex after a head injury. Which part of the brainstem does a normal response show is working?
options: The medulla oblongata
The pons
The midbrain
The cerebellum

q: Mr. Sato's spinal cord was completely cut at C5 an hour ago. His blood pressure is low, his heart rate is 48, and his feet are warm and pink. Which explanation fits all three findings?
options: His vagus nerve was cut, so vagal tone is lost
His adrenal medulla is releasing too much epinephrine
He has lost sympathetic tone while vagal output continues
His skeletal muscles are paralyzed, so they need less of the blood flow

q: Five minutes after a near-accident, a driver's sympathetic nerves have returned to resting activity, but her heart is still pounding and her hands shake. Why?
options: Epinephrine from the adrenal medulla is still circulating
Her vagal tone is still switched off
Norepinephrine lasts for hours in the gap at each varicosity
Her heart has lost its muscarinic receptor proteins

q: On a warm afternoon, a resting hiker's skin flushes and she sweats, yet her pupils do not widen and her gut keeps working. What does this show about the sympathetic division?
options: It acts only as an all-or-none mass discharge
Its output can be targeted at some effectors without the others
Sweating and skin blood flow are controlled by the parasympathetic division
Heat blocks the alpha-1 receptor proteins of the iris

q: A resting patient is given a drug that blocks the nicotinic receptor proteins in every autonomic ganglion. What happens to his heart rate?
options: It falls, because sympathetic input to the heart is removed
It stays the same, because the two effects cancel exactly
It rises, because removing both tones takes away the larger vagal brake
It stops, because the heart needs autonomic input to beat

q: A person lying down stands up quickly, and for a moment the pressure in her large arteries dips. Predict the change in each variable a few seconds later, as the reflex responds.

variables.name: Firing of stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the artery walls
Diameter of vessels in the skin and gut
